lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Ecosystem as a Self Sustaining Unit and Its Categories

pages.body:
Think about a small pond near your community or a patch of forest behind your school. Plants grow there, insects fly and animals feed, yet no one waters the plants or feeds the animals. The place seems to look after itself.

- What do you think keeps the pond or the forest going without human help?
- What would happen to the animals if all the plants in the place disappeared?

Living things never live alone. They live together with other organisms and with the non living things around them. In this lesson we define the ecosystem, explain why it is called self sustaining and learn the three categories of ecosystems.

We start with a clear meaning of the word ecosystem.

pages.title: What an ecosystem is
pages.body:
An ecosystem is a community of living organisms together with the non living things in their surroundings, all interacting with one another in a particular area. A pond, a forest, a grassland, a river, a farm and even a rotting log can each be an ecosystem. The living things in an ecosystem are called its biotic components. The non living things, such as water, light, air, soil and temperature, are called its abiotic components.

Next we explain how an ecosystem can keep running with very little supply from outside.

pages.title: Why an ecosystem is self sustaining
pages.body: An ecosystem is a self sustaining unit because it provides most of what its organisms need. Green plants and algae capture energy from sunlight and use it to make food. Animals get their food by eating plants or other animals. When plants and animals die or produce waste, decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break them down and return nutrients to the soil or water, where plants can use them again. So the nutrients keep moving in a cycle, and the only thing that must come from outside is a steady supply of energy from the Sun.

- Producers make food using sunlight.
- Consumers feed on producers or on other consumers.
- Decomposers break down dead matter and waste and return nutrients.
- Components interact with and depend on one another, so a change in one part can affect the others.

Ecosystems are grouped by where they are found. We study three categories.

pages.title: Categories of ecosystems
pages.body:
| **Category** | **Where it is found** | **Examples in Ghana** |
|---|---|---|
| Terrestrial ecosystem | On land | Forests such as Kakum, the savanna grassland of Mole National Park, farms, school compounds and rocky hills |
| Aquatic ecosystem | In water. Freshwater ecosystems have little salt and marine ecosystems have salty water | Ponds, streams, the Volta River, Lake Volta, Lake Bosomtwe, lagoons and the sea in the Gulf of Guinea |
| Arboreal ecosystem | In and on trees | The branches, leaves and trunk of a tall forest tree such as an odum or a mango tree |

We look at each category in turn, beginning with ecosystems on land.

pages.title: The terrestrial ecosystem
pages.body:
A terrestrial ecosystem is found on land. Its climate and soil decide the kind of plants that grow, and the plants decide the animals that can live there. A tropical rainforest has tall trees and high rainfall. A savanna has grasses and scattered trees, with a long dry season. Farms and gardens are also terrestrial ecosystems, though humans manage them.

Now we move into water.

pages.title: The aquatic ecosystem
pages.body:
An aquatic ecosystem is found in water. Because water holds heat well and supplies a lot of moisture, the temperature in water changes more slowly than on land. Light reaches only the upper layer, so tiny floating plants called phytoplankton grow near the surface and form the base of the food chain. Aquatic ecosystems are either freshwater, such as ponds, rivers and lakes, or marine, such as the sea and the ocean.

Finally we look at life in the trees.

pages.title: The arboreal ecosystem
pages.body:
An arboreal ecosystem is the ecosystem found on trees. A large tree supplies food, shelter and nesting places to many organisms. Birds nest in the branches, monkeys and squirrels move among the branches, tree frogs and chameleons rest on leaves, insects feed on leaves and bark, and plants such as ferns and orchids grow on the branches. Organisms of an arboreal ecosystem are adapted for climbing, gripping and moving at a height.

[[pic: Three panel illustration. Panel one shows a savanna terrestrial ecosystem. Panel two shows a pond aquatic ecosystem. Panel three shows a tall forest tree with birds, monkeys and insects as an arboreal ecosystem. Label each panel.]]

> **Did you know?** Lake Volta, created when the Akosombo Dam was built across the Volta River, is one of the largest man made lakes in the world by surface area. It is a freshwater aquatic ecosystem that supports a large fishing community.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Components of Ecosystems and How They Interact

pages.body:
Imagine that all the frogs in a pond suddenly disappear. For a few weeks nothing looks different, but soon there are more mosquitoes and the snakes that fed on the frogs begin to leave.

- Why do you think the loss of one kind of animal changed so many other things?
- What non living things in the pond might also be affected if the plants around it were cut down?

Every ecosystem is made of components that depend on one another. In this lesson we list the biotic and abiotic components of each category of ecosystem, compare the organisms that live in them and explain how the parts affect one another.

We begin with the living parts of an ecosystem, which are grouped by how they get their food.

pages.title: Biotic components
pages.body:
- Producers are green plants and algae that make their own food by photosynthesis. Grass, cocoa trees and floating algae are producers.
- Consumers get food by eating other organisms. Herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals and omnivores eat both. A grasshopper, a lion and a human being are examples of a herbivore, a carnivore and an omnivore respectively.
- Decomposers are bacteria and fungi that feed on dead organisms and waste and return nutrients to the soil or water. Mushrooms growing on a rotten log are decomposers at work.

Next we list the non living parts that set the conditions for life in an ecosystem.

pages.title: Abiotic components
pages.body:
- Sunlight supplies the energy that producers use to make food.
- Temperature affects how fast organisms grow and which ones can live in a place.
- Water is needed by every organism and, in aquatic ecosystems, forms the habitat itself.
- Air supplies oxygen for respiration and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. In water, dissolved oxygen is the form that animals use.
- Soil supplies mineral salts and anchors plants. In aquatic ecosystems the mud at the bottom has a similar role.
- Wind and rainfall affect water supply, temperature and the spread of seeds.

Here we put the biotic and abiotic components of the three categories side by side.

pages.title: Components found in each category
pages.body:
| **Category** | **Biotic components** | **Abiotic components** |
|---|---|---|
| Terrestrial | Grass, trees, shrubs, grasshoppers, rodents, snakes, birds, antelopes, mushrooms and bacteria in the soil | Sunlight, air, soil, rainfall, temperature, wind and rocks |
| Aquatic | Algae, water plants, water insects, tadpoles, tilapia and catfish, frogs, kingfishers and bacteria in the mud | Water, dissolved oxygen, sunlight reaching the surface, temperature, mud and dissolved mineral salts |
| Arboreal | Tree leaves and fruits, epiphytic plants, caterpillars and ants, tree frogs, chameleons, monkeys, squirrels and nesting birds, and fungi on bark | Sunlight in the canopy, rain, wind, tree bark and branches, air and temperature |

Now we see how the organisms in each category differ because their surroundings differ.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Differences among organisms in the categories

pages.title: Differences among organisms in the categories
pages.body:
- Terrestrial organisms such as antelopes and grasshoppers have legs or wings for moving on land. Many plants have roots that reach for water in the soil and waxy leaves that reduce water loss.
- Aquatic organisms such as tilapia have gills for taking in dissolved oxygen, fins and a streamlined body for swimming. Many water plants have thin leaves or float on the surface where there is light.
- Arboreal organisms such as monkeys and squirrels have strong limbs, gripping hands and often a tail for balance. Many birds have claws for perching and wings for moving between branches.

Finally we study how each component acts on the others, because that is what makes the ecosystem work as one unit.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How the components affect one another

pages.title: How the components affect one another
pages.body:
Abiotic factors affect living things. Rainfall decides how well grass grows. Light decides how deep algae can live in a pond. Temperature decides which animals can live on a mountain or in a lagoon.

Living things affect the abiotic factors. Plants shade the soil and lower its temperature. Fallen leaves decay into humus that improves the soil. Plant roots hold soil together and reduce erosion. Algae in a pond add oxygen to the water during photosynthesis.

Living things affect one another. Organisms are linked by feeding, and these links form food chains. A food chain begins with a producer and shows the direction in which energy moves.

- Terrestrial food chain, grass to grasshopper to toad to snake to eagle.
- Aquatic food chain, algae to small fish to catfish to kingfisher.
- Arboreal food chain, leaves to caterpillar to tree frog to tree snake.

[[pic: Food web for a pond ecosystem showing algae, water plants, tadpoles, small fish, tilapia, catfish, kingfisher and bacteria in the mud. Arrows show the direction of energy flow.]]

Organisms also compete for light, water, food and space, and some organisms help one another, for example when bees pollinate flowers and receive nectar in return. If one component changes, the others change too. When forest trees are cut down, the monkeys and birds lose food and shelter, the soil is exposed to heat and erosion, and the number of decomposers falls. This is why we must protect every part of an ecosystem.

pages.body:
- An ecosystem is a community of living organisms together with the non living things around them, interacting in a particular area.
- An ecosystem is self sustaining because producers capture sunlight, consumers feed on other organisms and decomposers return nutrients. Only energy from the Sun needs to come from outside.
- Ecosystems are grouped into terrestrial ecosystems on land, aquatic ecosystems in water and arboreal ecosystems in trees.
- Biotic components are producers, consumers and decomposers. Abiotic components include sunlight, temperature, water, air and soil.
- Organisms of each category have features that suit their habitat.
- Components affect one another through abiotic effects on living things, living effects on abiotic things and feeding links.
- A change in one component of an ecosystem affects the other components.
